full_judgment: 19. When the parties to an action has expressly and by implication waived or has foregone the right and has come to a consensus to resolve the dispute by any lawful agreement or compromise or even by conduct, they/he cannot challenge such action/order on the ground of acquiescence, waiver and estoppel as well as such order having been passed where he was a party and never raised any objection rather on consent of both the parties, he cannot now raise any objection of pecuniary jurisdiction specially when he kept silent throughout the proceeding and specially when the order has been passed on coin-promise between all other parties and now by preferring this appeal he cannot for the first time raise this issue. In a case reported in 1993 MLR 247=PLD 1984 Quetta 92 it has been held 'where the appeal lay to the District Judge but was filed in the High Court and no objection was raised by the respondent in respect of the procedure and raised only when the decision went against him that irregular mode adopted by the High Court in entertaining the appeal had not resulted in prejudicing the merit of the case. Therefore, the decision of the High Court did not merit reversal.' Though the general principle is 'if the Court has no jurisdiction, no amount of waiver or consent can confer jurisdiction on the Court' but, a distinction must be made between "patent" and "latent" want of jurisdiction, in one, submission to the jurisdiction cannot cure the defect, while in the other, no objection to want of juris-diction can be taken at a later stage if the objection is not taken at the earliest (Altaf Hossain Vs. Chief Settlement Commissioner 18 DLR(SC)164). Again in the case of Sharafat Vs. Dr. Islamuddin (1998 BLD 92) it has been held that 'when a case has been decided on merit, it should not be reversed unless it has resulted in failure of justice'. In the case of Kiran Singh Vs. Chaman (A 1954 SC 340 1 SCR 117) it has been observed that a case tried on merits Should not be liable to be reversed purely on technical grounds, unless it has resulted in failure of justice, and the policy of the legislature has been to treat objections to jurisdiction, both territorial and pecuniary, as technical". Under the Indian jurisdiction, in a series of decisions, it has been held 'when a case is disposed of on merit, no interference by the Appellate or Revisional Court on technical ground of territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction is called for unless prejudiced (AIR 1983 Mad 9). In AIR 1984 Punj 345 it has been held 'lack of pecuniary jurisdiction is no inherent lack of jurisdiction.' Apart from the aforementioned series of decisions on the question of lack of jurisdiction it appears that the predecessor of the present appellant having transferred his entire share in the property in question by registered instruments, his heir, the appellant, cannot now challenge the same before this Division after 25 years of keeping the property under mortgage to the bank against a loan or by transfer without proving his title and possession over the suit land.
